expect: Mastering: Identifies key differences (permanence vs. temporariness of change, propaganda vs. reality); uses own knowledge to evaluate both (19 million women employed 1944, Rosie the Riveter imagery for A; post-war pressure to return home, lower pay than male counterparts, 1950s domestic ideology for B); explains why interpretations differ (contemporary vs. retrospective evidence, feminist vs. traditional perspective). Secure: Explains differences with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Identifies some differences and supports one. Emerging: Summarises each without explaining differences.
value: This question always gives you two sources. Mastering: Compares the two sources directly, setting out where they agree and where they differ (permanence vs. temporariness of change, propaganda vs. reality); tests both against own knowledge (19 million women employed 1944, Rosie the Riveter imagery for A; post-war pressure to return home, lower pay than male counterparts, 1950s domestic ideology for B); explains why the two views differ (contemporary vs. retrospective evidence, feminist vs. traditional perspective). Secure: Compares both sources with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Uses one source well and refers to the other. Emerging: Describes each source in turn without comparing them.

expect: Mastering: Explains the significance of the Tulsa Massacre in showing the scale of organised racial violence (at least 36 dead, 35 blocks destroyed); the active role of deputised civilians and the failure of authorities to protect Black residents; the deliberate suppression of the event from public memory for decades; and what this reveals about the systematic nature of racial violence rather than isolated incidents. Secure: Two or more dimensions explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One dimension explained, others listed. Emerging: General statement about the massacre’s seriousness without explanation.
value: Mastering: Explains the significance of the Tulsa Massacre in showing the scale of organised racial violence (at least 39 dead, 35 blocks destroyed); the active role of deputised civilians and the failure of authorities to protect Black residents; the deliberate suppression of the event from public memory for decades; and what this reveals about the systematic nature of racial violence rather than isolated incidents.
